title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline on intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, K=200 paired tasks were sampled deterministically and a single shared generator output per task was evaluated in both arms (shared_initial_generation). The requested model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...), and all model/provider traces, validator outputs, and execution manifests were archived (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...). Observed primary outcome: baseline success = 200/200, guarded success = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair pathway was never invoked. We release the full preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...), execution, and analysis artifacts for replay and discuss design choices, the ceiling interpretation, and implications for future verifier‑value evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation is an active NetOps/AIOps research direction, but stochastic generators (LLMs) can produce changes that cause regressions when applied live. A common mitigation is the generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architecture: the generator proposes a candidate, a verifier/emulator checks it, and an automated repair step attempts correction if the verifier rejects. Prior work suggests this pipeline can reduce regressions, yet claims are sensitive to dataset composition, validator coverage, and generator error rates. To provide an artifact‑grounded, preregistered estimate of the verifier+repair marginal effect, we designed a paired confirmatory experiment that holds generator output fixed across arms: each sampled intent yields a single shared candidate; that candidate is scored directly in the baseline arm and is passed to the verifier (and repaired only if preregistered rules permit) in the guarded arm. This design isolates the verifier’s marginal impact on the binary apply outcome (validator‑compliant apply vs regression). The study was fully preregistered (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) and executed with comprehensive provenance and immutable artifacts.
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps research has converged on generate→validate→repair evaluation pipelines and on separating translation tasks from formal reasoning/verification. Representative contributions motivate verifier‑guided automation and synthesized benchmark suites that exercise LLMs at scale (e.g., Cornetto and related generate‑validate‑repair pipelines). Surveys and position papers emphasize workflow‑centred evaluation and argue that reliable automation depends on the machinery around LLMs (tool orchestration, verifiers, and deterministic validators). Our experiment differs: it is a preregistered, paired, artifact‑archived comparison that isolates marginal verifier value by using a single shared generator output per task and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). This contrasts with prior work that often evaluates interactive or multi‑call agentic systems where the generator and validator interact, making marginal attribution difficult.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in regression‑causing change rate). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 posited a lower regression rate in the guarded arm. Power assumptions (preregistered) targeted a baseline regression rate of 0.20 and a target absolute reduction of 0.08 (alpha=0.05, power=0.80); sensitivity scenarios across baseline rates were included in the preregistration. All preregistration metadata are archived (preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...).
Deterministic paired design and sampling. Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and filtered to those covered by the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Sampling was deterministic: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, and select the first K=200 tasks. This deterministic selection and fixed generator seed ensure exact reproducibility; task_manifest.jsonl and execution/task_manifest.jsonl record generator ids, seeds, and task_payloads (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 f1d447b7...).
Shared initial generation. For each task we performed a single shared generator call (shared_initial_generation) using the requested_model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 1acce925...). That single candidate configuration was used in both arms: baseline (accept-and-score) and guarded (validator checks; if invalid, preregistered policy allowed a single repair call). The model call budget allowed up to maximum_model_calls=400; the run used model_calls_used=200 because the single shared generation per task sufficed (execution manifest SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6...). All provider call traces are archived (execution/provider_calls/*.json).
Validator semantics, scoring, and repair policy. The validator parses textual candidates into structured command sequences and applies deterministic safety and dependency checks (examples: shutdown→MTU change patterns, group minimum‑up constraints). The scorer id deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0) writes a per‑episode JSON trace with normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshot, violation_codes, and repair_applied boolean. The primary outcome uses scoring_rule full_intent_constraint_validation; every scoring JSON is archived under execution/scoring/*.json. The guarded policy permits exactly one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1) and revalidation once; repair traces would be stored under execution/repair_traces/* if any repairs occurred. In this execution repair_applied==false for all tasks.
Execution provenance and integrity. All raw responses, provider traces, scoring outputs, and execution logs were persisted and hashed. Key artifact hashes included: raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6..., model configuration SHA‑256 1acce925..., transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 79c91155..., and master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...; full hash manifests are in execution/execution_manifest.json. The run followed the preregistered missingness, contamination, and retry rules; any exclusions or retries are logged in execution/execution_log.jsonl.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The run completed per preregistration: started 2026-08-27T11:26:03.764166Z, completed 2026-08-27T11:49:04.685661Z (execution manifest). Planned episodes = 400 (two arms × K=200); completed episodes = 400; failed episodes = 0. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generation per task) and hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 (provider audit).
Primary confirmatory outcome. Observed counts: complete_pairs = 200, baseline_success_count = 200, guarded_success_count = 200. Paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...). The paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. We executed the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test: p = 1.00. We computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed=1729 as preregistered); the CI is [0.00,0.00] (analysis artifacts recorded). All per‑task scoring JSONs report validator.valid==true and violation_count==0; representative scoring traces are archived (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json, etc.).
Repair loop and cost accounting. The guarded repair pathway was never invoked: repair_applied=false across all 200 guarded episodes. Consequently the repair call budget and repair latency were unused; there is no observed latency or cost difference across arms beyond the single shared generation. Provider call audit and cache metadata confirm no cross‑condition cache reuse or stateful provider anomalies (execution/provider_calls/* and execution/call_cache/*). The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact documents internal accounting consistency and confirms all deterministic checks passed.
Representative examples. Five representative tasks and their archived traces illustrate common operational patterns in the task pool: MTU migration with safe shutdown/restore (task-000001), make‑before‑break uplink switchover (task-000002), paired MTU equalization (task-000003), safe VLAN transfer (task-000004), and failover‑then‑retire uplink VLAN edit (task-000005). For each, the shared generator output equals the normalized_reference_answer and the validator trace records parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, and a final_state snapshot (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; responses: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt).
sections.discussion:
Null result interpretation and ceiling effect. The observed null (paired difference = 0.00 with CI [0.00,0.00]) reflects a ceiling effect under the chosen sample and components: the deterministic generator outputs satisfied the deterministic validator constraints for every sampled intent, so the verifier had no opportunity to alter the binary apply outcome. This is a valid, reproducible outcome under the preregistered contract but does not imply verifiers are universally redundant. Rather, it demonstrates that when generator accuracy on validator‑covered intents is already perfect (in our synthetic pool and chosen model), an inserted verifier+repair module produces no marginal benefit for the binary validator‑compliance endpoint used here.
Design lessons for future confirmatory evaluations. To reveal verifier/repair value, experimenters should (i) select task pools with nontrivial baseline error rates (e.g., include intents at the validator coverage boundary or real operator‑written intents), (ii) evaluate weaker or multiple generator models to avoid generator ceiling effects, (iii) design interactive generator–verifier protocols that permit the generator to adapt to verifier feedback (our shared_initial_generation design intentionally prevented generator adaptation to isolate marginal verifier effect), or (iv) measure continuous operational outcomes (blast radius, partial regressions, or latent metric degradations) rather than a single binary validator verdict. Each alternative changes the estimand and requires a correspondingly revised preregistration and power plan.
Threats to validity and artifacts for external audit. Internal validity: preserved by deterministic sampling, seeds, and deterministic validator traces; all artifacts and hashes (execution/* and analysis/*) are archived for replay. Construct validity: the primary endpoint measures validator compliance—its operational meaning depends on validator fidelity; we document validator rules and per‑task violation codes in scoring artifacts to allow reviewers to assess construct alignment. External validity: single requested model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and filtered validator coverage limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power assumptions (baseline 0.20) were violated by the observed baseline=1.0; we therefore report exact tests and bootstrap CIs rather than rely on the original power calculation. All these points and the underlying artifact locations are recorded in the manuscript evidence bundle for independent inspection.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison of a G→V→R pipeline vs an LLM‑only pipeline on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks. Under the specific model, generator, and deterministic validator used, both arms produced 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; the repair loop was never invoked and the paired estimate is exactly zero (McNemar p=1.00; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]). This ceiling outcome highlights that demonstrating verifier value requires failure‑rich, realistically heterogeneous task pools or experimental designs that allow generator–verifier interaction. We provide the complete preregistration, execution traces, validator logs, and analysis artifacts to enable replay, secondary analyses, and alternative experiment designs that probe verifier benefit under different, operationally realistic regimes.

limitations: Single requested model (gpt-5-mini) — findings do not generalize to other LLMs without further experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: observed baseline success = 100% prevented demonstration of verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
